strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored problem: robustness of skill-based meta-RL to noisy offline demonstrations, which is a realistic concern for real-world offline datasets.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across four long-horizon multi-task environments (Kitchen, Office, Maze2D, AntMaze) with multiple controlled noise levels, showing consistent improvements over SPiRL/SiMPL and other baselines.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component (online buffer, offline buffer, prioritization/relabeling, exploration policy) as well as sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters (temperature T, KLD coefficient) across all noise levels.
Good qualitative analysis and visualizations (t-SNE task/skill embeddings, trajectory visualizations, evolution of control factor β) that help interpret why and how the method works.
Detailed reproducibility materials: full derivations of parameterized losses, network architectures, hyperparameter tables, and dataset construction procedures in the appendix.
The dynamic balancing mechanism (β) between offline and online data based on relative return quality is an intuitively reasonable and empirically validated design choice.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the paper largely recombines existing components (RND-based exploration, prioritized/return-based filtering, reward-model relabeling, SPiRL/SiMPL skill learning) rather than introducing a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the 'maximum return relabeling' is essentially reward-model-based return estimation combined with softmax prioritization, a fairly standard technique in offline RL.

No comparison against dedicated noise-robust imitation/RL methods that the related work section itself cites as relevant (e.g., Sasaki & Yamashina 2020, Mandlekar et al. 2022, Yu et al. 2024); all baselines are either non-robust meta-RL/skill methods or naive exploration additions (RND), making it hard to assess PRISM's advantage over methods specifically designed for noisy demonstrations.

Two of the four evaluation environments (Office and AntMaze) are newly introduced by the authors themselves, and the Maze2D offline dataset differs from the original SiMPL setup (fewer tasks, incomplete map coverage), which the authors acknowledge lowers baseline performance relative to prior reported results — this raises concerns about fair baseline reproduction and potential benchmark-construction bias favoring the proposed method.

The method requires simultaneously training many components per task (exploration policy, task-specific reward model, online buffer, high-level policy, shared low-level skill model), which likely incurs substantially higher computational/memory cost than SiMPL/SPiRL; while the paper claims comparable per-iteration cost, no wall-clock time or resource comparison is provided.

Robustness is only tested against homogeneous, zero-mean Gaussian action noise; more realistic or structured noise patterns (e.g., systematic bias, sensor dropout, sparse corruption, adversarial noise) are not considered, limiting claims of general real-world robustness.

The reward model used for maximum return relabeling is trained only on exploration/online data (which itself may be limited early in training) and its estimation accuracy/calibration is never directly validated, leaving open the possibility of relabeling errors propagating into skill prioritization.

Only mean ± std over 5 seeds is reported without statistical significance testing, and some improvements (e.g., Maze2D Expert vs. SiMPL) are within overlapping error bars, weakening the strength of some empirical claims.

The paper is dense with notation and the main text sometimes just points to the appendix for essential implementation details (e.g., parameterized losses), which could hinder readability and quick assessment of core technical contributions.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored problem: robustness of skill-based meta-RL to noisy offline demonstrations, which is practically relevant.
Extensive empirical evaluation across four long-horizon environments (Kitchen, Office, Maze2D, AntMaze) and multiple noise levels, with 5-seed averaging.
Thorough ablation studies (component removal, prioritization temperature T, KLD coefficient) and appendix material providing implementation and hyperparameter details that aid reproducibility.
Qualitative visualizations (t-SNE task/skill embeddings, trajectory plots, evolution of the control factor beta) that help illustrate the intended mechanism of skill refinement.
Consistent, sizeable performance gains over SPiRL/SiMPL baselines at higher noise levels in the reported experiments.
weaknesses: Missing baselines: the paper explicitly cites prior work on noisy/robust imitation learning and behavior cloning from noisy demonstrations (Sasaki & Yamashina 2020; Mandlekar et al. 2022; Chae et al. 2022; Yu et al. 2024) as motivation, yet none of these are compared against empirically — only SPiRL/SiMPL without noise-handling are used as skill-based baselines, making it hard to assess whether PRISM outperforms existing noise-robust approaches or just naive skill learning.

Two of the four evaluation environments (Office, AntMaze) are newly introduced by the authors themselves, and the Maze2D setup differs from the original SiMPL benchmark (fewer tasks, incomplete map coverage) with results acknowledged to be lower than published SiMPL numbers — this raises concerns about cherry-picked or self-designed benchmarks favoring the proposed method and complicates fair comparison.

Limited methodological novelty: the framework largely combines existing components (RND-based exploration, prioritized/return-based replay filtering, SPiRL skill learning, SiMPL hierarchical meta-RL, learned reward models for relabeling) without a clearly novel algorithmic or theoretical contribution beyond their integration.

Computational/scalability concerns: PRISM trains a separate exploration policy and reward model per training task, which could scale poorly with the number of tasks; the paper's efficiency argument (separate iteration counting) is somewhat superficial and doesn't address memory/compute growth with task count.

The reward model used for maximum return relabeling requires reasonably accurate reward supervision from online rollouts, which may be difficult to obtain reliably in truly noisy/sparse real-world settings that motivate the paper; this potential circularity/assumption is not discussed.

No statistical significance testing beyond showing standard deviations; given the relatively small gains in some settings (e.g., Maze2D expert/low-noise cases), it's unclear if improvements are robust.

The periodic performance drops from high-level policy reinitialization every K_iter (visible in Fig. 6) are not well justified or compared against alternative designs (e.g., warm-starting instead of reinitializing).
Claims of relevance to "real-world noisy scenarios" are not substantiated by any real-robot or real-world experiments; all evaluation is simulation-based.

The paper's per-task components (exploration policy, reward model) somewhat undercut the meta-learning framing, since much of the added machinery operates independently per task rather than being shared/meta-learned across tasks.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored problem: robustness of skill-based meta-RL to noisy/suboptimal offline demonstrations, with a clear failure-mode analysis (corrupted skill library propagating to the high-level policy).

Extensive empirical evaluation across four long-horizon environments (Kitchen, Office, Maze2D, AntMaze) and multiple noise levels/types (Gaussian noise at varying sigma, random action injection, medium/random quality datasets, limited dataset sizes), showing consistent improvements over SPiRL and SiMPL baselines.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each component (online buffer, offline buffer, prioritization/relabeling, skill-improvement policy, RND, high-level re-initialization, temperature T, KLD coefficient), which supports the claimed design choices.

Good supplementary analyses (t-SNE of skill and task representations, trajectory visualizations, mixing coefficient β dynamics, reward model stability) that provide qualitative insight into why/how the method works.
Reasonable attention to reproducibility: detailed algorithm boxes, hyperparameter tables, environment descriptions, and code availability statement.
Computational overhead is quantified and shown to be modest (16% per-iteration increase during meta-train only, no meta-test overhead), which is a fair and transparent limitation discussion.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the method largely combines existing ingredients (RND-based exploration, prioritized/return-based replay, reward-model-based relabeling, periodic skill re-training) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the core contribution is more of an engineering integration tailored to the noisy-offline-skill setting.

No comparison against other noise-robust imitation learning / offline RL methods cited in the related work (e.g., Sasaki & Yamashina 2020, Mandlekar et al. 2022, Yu et al. 2024a) applied as a preprocessing step before SiMPL, which would help isolate whether the gains come from something specific to the proposed skill-refinement framework versus generic noise-robust demonstration filtering.

The approach requires online reward signals for training the reward model and high-level policy during meta-training (as in SiMPL), so the robustness claim is specific to noise in the reward-free offline skill data; this scope is reasonable but could be stated more prominently as a limiting assumption relative to fully offline noisy-reward settings.

The framework has many interacting components and hyperparameters (Kiter, T, λ_imp^kld, δ_ext/δ_int, buffer sizes), and although ablations are provided, the practical burden of tuning across new environments/tasks is non-trivial and only partially mitigated by the heuristic of scaling T with max return.

Two of the four evaluation environments (Office, AntMaze) are newly introduced by the authors rather than standard benchmarks, and the offline data is synthetically noised expert/oracle trajectories in all cases, which may not fully capture the structured, non-Gaussian noise patterns of real-world data despite the random-injection experiment attempting to address this.

Table 1 and several figures are dense and could benefit from clearer statistical reporting (e.g., significance tests) given the relatively small number of seeds (5) for many closely-spaced noise-level comparisons.

The scale of task distributions (e.g., 25-40 meta-train tasks) is modest, leaving open questions about scalability of the self-improving refinement process to larger and more diverse task/skill libraries.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: robustness of skill-based meta-RL to noisy/suboptimal offline demonstrations, with a clear motivating example (Fig. 2) showing failure modes of prior work.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four long-horizon environments (Kitchen, Office, Maze2D, AntMaze) and multiple noise levels, with consistent improvements over SPiRL/SiMPL and non-skill baselines.

Thorough ablation studies (component removal, temperature T, KLD coefficient, RND, re-initialization) and additional robustness checks (limited dataset size, random action injection, diverse sub-optimal data) that substantiate the claimed robustness rather than relying on a single headline result.
Good reproducibility: detailed algorithm boxes, hyperparameter tables, network architectures, and released code; reward model stability and computational overhead are explicitly analyzed.
Useful qualitative/diagnostic visualizations (t-SNE of skills and task embeddings, buffer mixing coefficient dynamics, trajectory visualizations) that help interpret why the method works.
weaknesses: The 'reward-free offline skill learning' framing is partially undermined: SISL relies heavily on dense online reward signals and per-task reward models/improvement policies during meta-training, making it more of a hybrid offline-online method than a pure offline-noise-robust skill learner; this weakens the comparison to methods that use only reward-free offline data.

Method complexity is high (decoupled improvement policy, RND-based intrinsic reward, multiple buffers, periodic skill re-training with high-level policy reinitialization, per-task reward models), raising concerns about scalability to larger task sets (separate πimp/Qimp/reward-model machinery per training task) and about practical tunability beyond the studied hyperparameters.

Novelty is somewhat incremental — it largely combines existing ideas (RND exploration, prioritized/return-based relabeling, curriculum via buffer mixing) within the skill-based meta-RL pipeline rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

Empirical comparison is limited to SiMPL/SPiRL and generic meta-RL baselines; more recent skill-based meta-RL methods cited in related work (e.g., Chien & Lai 2023, Cho & Sun 2024, He et al. 2024) are not empirically compared, leaving it unclear whether SISL's gains hold against stronger contemporaries.

Two of the four environments (Office, AntMaze) are newly introduced by the authors themselves, which somewhat limits independent validation of the claimed generality, and the noise model (Gaussian perturbation of an oracle/expert policy) is a synthetic proxy for real-world noise, only partially mitigated by the random-injection and sub-optimal-dataset appendices.

The claim of being the 'first' to address noisy demonstrations in skill-based meta-RL is a strong, somewhat overreaching statement given adjacent work on noisy imitation/offline RL is only partially discussed and not benchmarked.

Statistical robustness is based on only 5 seeds, and some ablation results (e.g., Fig. 8, Fig. G.1) show error bars that appear to overlap across variants, making some component-level claims less conclusive.
